hints: Sketch cuminyl alcohol and mark the plane of symmetry through the two opposite ring substituents, then count how many ring carbons are paired as identical.
walkthrough:
Think in carbon environments, not total carbons**
Remember, in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR every peak is a different chemical environment. If two carbons can be swapped by symmetry they give one shared peak. Cuminyl alcohol has formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ with 10 carbons in total, but many are equivalent.

Count the ring, then the side chains**
Look at the para-disubstituted ring. The two substituted carbons are each unique, that is 2 environments. The remaining four ring $\text{CH}$ carbons form two identical pairs, that is 2 more environments. So the ring gives 4 peaks. Then add the side chains: $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ gives 1, the isopropyl $\text{CH}$ gives 1, and the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the isopropyl group are identical and give 1 shared peak. $4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7$ peaks.

hints: Compare the two structures side by side and list which functional group is unique to each, $\text{CHO}$ versus $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
Recall the characteristic IR wavenumber ranges for a carbonyl double bond and for a hydrogen bonded alcohol O-H or single C-O bond.
walkthrough:
Spot what is different, ignore what is shared**
Both molecules have the same benzene ring and the same isopropyl group, so $\text{C-H}$, $\text{C-C}$ and aromatic absorptions appear in both spectra and are useless for telling them apart. Focus only on $\text{-CHO}$ in cuminaldehyde versus $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ in cuminyl alcohol.

Assign the diagnostic absorptions**
Cuminaldehyde contains a carbonyl, so you see a strong sharp $\text{C=O}$ stretch at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ which is absent in the alcohol. Cuminyl alcohol contains an alcohol group, so you see a broad $\text{O-H}$ stretch at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (due to hydrogen bonding) and a $\text{C-O}$ stretch at 1000-1260 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, both absent in the aldehyde.

Final answer: Bond in cuminaldehyde only: $\text{C=O}$ at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
Bond in cuminyl alcohol only: $\text{O-H}$ at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ (or $\text{C-O}$ at 1000-1260 $\text{cm}^{-1}$).

hints: For step 1, recognise addition of an isopropyl group to benzene and recall which catalyst and electrophile source installs an alkyl group on a benzene ring.
For step 2, recognise addition of a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group para to the alkyl group and recall the acyl chloride plus Lewis acid combination.
For step 3, recognise conversion of $\text{-COCH}_3$ to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ and think of the methyl ketone test that cleaves this group.
For step 4, recognise conversion of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol and recall which powerful hydride reagent is required, and why $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not enough.
walkthrough:
Install the isopropyl group by Friedel-Crafts alkylation**
Benzene to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ is alkylation. Use 2-chloropropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCl}$, with the Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ and heat to generate the $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ electrophile. Propene with acid catalysis is an accepted alternative source of the same electrophile.

Install the ethanoyl group by Friedel-Crafts acylation**
The isopropylbenzene to 4-isopropyl phenyl methyl ketone change adds $\text{COCH}_3$ para to the alkyl group. The isopropyl group is 2,6-directing and activates the ring, so para substitution dominates. Use ethanoyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, with $\text{AlCl}_3$ and heat to form the $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{=O}$ electrophile: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2 + \text{HCl}$.

Shorten the methyl ketone to a carboxylic acid**
$\text{-COCH}_3$ to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ is the haloform reaction. Heat with $\text{I}_2$ in $\text{NaOH}$ (iodoform conditions, $\text{Cl}_2$ also works) to give the carboxylate plus $\text{CHI}_3$, then add dilute acid $\text{H}^+$ to protonate to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$: $\text{RCOCH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CHI}_3 + 3\text{NaI} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Reduce the acid to the primary alcohol**
$\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ needs a very strong reducing agent. Use lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$, in dry ether (water would destroy the reagent), followed by dilute acid work up. Do not use $\text{NaBH}_4$ here, it is too weak to reduce a carboxylic acid.

hints: For step 2, think about what type of species attacks the benzene pi system when $\text{AlCl}_3$ activates an acyl chloride.
For step 4, think about what happens to the oxidation level of carbon when $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ in terms of gain of hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Classify the ring acylation**
In step 2 the benzene pi cloud attacks a positive acylium electrophile, $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{=O}$, then loses $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity. Attack by an electrophile on an aromatic ring followed by substitution of hydrogen is electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Classify the acid to alcohol change**
In step 4 the carboxyl carbon gains hydrogen (or loses oxygen) going from $\text{RCO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{RCH}_2\text{OH}$. Gain of hydrogen with hydride is reduction, even though no change in the benzene ring occurs.

Final answer: mechanism of step 2: electrophilic (aromatic) substitution;
type of reaction in step 4: reduction.
